doc.title: Derek Brown interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 5, 2021

title: Sweets Edison on originality and the saxophone lineage
summary: Rowe quotes Harry Edison on being an originator rather than an imitator and asks how to find a sound after Coltrane.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: All right. Well speaking of sweet spot, your description of developing your thing reminded me of a quote. I was able to interview Harry “Sweets” Edison, the trumpet player from the Basie era. And he was talking about when he was a young man, this would have been the late 1930s, he said this about the already-established musicians like Louis Armstrong and Coleman Hawkins. And what he said was, “Everybody had a sound of their own, a sound that could be recognized. That was our ambition in my day, to not © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
be an imitator, but an originator. We would rather be the world’s worst originator than the world’s greatest imitator.
Yeah. I can resonate with that.

Yeah. I was thinking about your sound and then the incredible breadth of saxophone sounds that have happened since the 20s. And so you’re in the lineage, you’re in the current lineage of what’s going on now. Because sometimes I wonder does it get harder to come up with your own sound? I mean how do you go beyond John Coltrane’s harmonic innovations and so if I can’t do that what can I do?
